title: AI Incident Response: The Council Measurement Framework
context: 2026-09-01 — EU AI Act Article 62 (serious incident reporting) and Article 73 (market surveillance) are approaching their application dates. Organisations need an incident-response posture that is auditable, not just documented. The Council of AI measurement framework applies the verified credential model to incident handling.
body: AI incident response in 2026 is no longer about having a written plan — it is about producing a verifiable record that the plan was followed. Three regulatory vectors converge: EU AI Act Article 62 requires high-risk AI system providers to report serious incidents to the market surveillance authority within 15 days; Article 73 gives authorities the power to request documentation and conduct inspections; and the Council of AI Containment Incident Index provides a public, append-only register of boundary events. A coherent incident-response posture under these vectors requires three measurement-integrated steps. (1) Detection: boundary instrumentation logs every inference, tool call, and output deviation — a serious incident is defined as a boundary crossing that the monitored containment instrumentation captured with a signed timestamp. The detection is itself a verified measurement: the system did not 'notice' the incident; it produced a signed record of the crossing. (2) Triage and containment: within 15 days, the provider must assess whether the incident meets the Article 62 notification threshold (death, serious harm, or large-scale irreversible damage). The triage decision is documented as a signed verdict — a measurement of severity against the regulatory threshold — so an auditor can later verify that the decision to report (or not) was made against the correct standard at the correct time. (3) Remediation and closure: the provider publishes a closure record into the Containment Incident Index, linked to the original detection. Together, the three records — detection, triage, closure — form an auditable incident chain. An Article 73 inspector does not need to trust the provider's incident log; they can verify each record's signature independently. The posture is monitored containment applied to incident response: you cannot prove no incident will ever occur, but you can prove — through a chain of signed, timestamped measurements — that every incident that was detected was handled against a stated process with an auditable outcome. For organisations preparing for the Article 62/73 application dates, this framework converts a compliance obligation into a verifiable operational discipline.
